planting.note: Grow as a cool, shaded greenhouse or air-conditioned houseplant specimen in a fine bark-and-sphagnum mix or small basket; White Masdevallia is a high-elevation Venezuelan cloud-forest species that needs consistently cool nights (50-60F) and cannot tolerate the warm, dry conditions of an average home.

directions: Grow in a cool, deeply shaded spot with constant high humidity and strong air movement, potted in a fine, fast-draining mix of small bark and live sphagnum moss; Masdevallia tovarensis comes from cloud forests near Tovar, Venezuela, at elevations where nights stay cool year-round, and it declines quickly wherever daytime highs regularly exceed the low 80s. Unlike its brightly colored cousins, this species produces pure white, waxy, long-lasting flowers held in pairs on slender, arching stems that can rebloom from the same spike for several years running. Keep the mix evenly moist at all times, since Masdevallia has no pseudobulbs to store water and shrivels quickly if allowed to dry out. Because of its narrow cool-growing requirements, it is best suited to a shaded greenhouse, enclosed porch, or air-conditioned room rather than an average heated home.

planting.note: Grow in a hanging basket or slatted pot, since Dracula flowers dangle downward from the base of the plant and would be blocked by a solid pot; use a fine, well-drained mix of small bark and sphagnum and keep in a cool, shaded, humid spot, as this Ecuadorian cloud-forest species cannot tolerate heat.

directions: Mount or grow in a hanging slatted basket filled with a fine, quick-draining bark-and-sphagnum mix, since the pendant flower spikes of Dracula simia emerge from the base of the plant and grow straight downward through the container. Native to cool, misty cloud forests on the slopes of the Ecuadorian Andes, this species became famous for its uncanny flower, whose two long tails and dark hairy centers combine with the shape of the fused sepals to resemble a small monkey's face, a resemblance widely noted in botanical and popular writing alike. It requires cool temperatures year-round, deep shade, and constant high humidity, and struggles or declines quickly if exposed to the warm daytime temperatures typical of a standard home. Keep the mix constantly moist and never let the shallow root system dry out, since Dracula species lack water-storing pseudobulbs and are unforgiving of drought.

planting.note: Set pseudobulbs half-buried in a gritty, humus-rich, well-drained mix in a shallow pan in early spring before roots emerge; Pleione bulbocodioides is among the hardiest ground orchids and can survive outdoors with a deep dry mulch in mild zone 6-7 gardens, but performs most reliably as a cold-frame or unheated greenhouse pot plant farther north.

directions: Half-bury the flattened pseudobulbs in a gritty mix of fine bark, leaf mold, and perlite in a shallow pan or raised bed in a lightly shaded spot, setting new bulbs out in earliest spring just before growth resumes. Pleione bulbocodioides comes from high-elevation grassland and rocky slopes across central and southern China, and each pseudobulb sends up a single vivid magenta-pink to rose-purple flower with a fringed, spotted lip before the pleated leaf has fully unfurled, giving plantings an unusually early, crocus-like burst of color. Water sparingly as flower buds appear, then increase watering through the growing season and taper off sharply as the leaf yellows in autumn so the pseudobulb can enter a firm, dry winter dormancy. This species tolerates more cold than most Pleiones and is often grown as a genuinely hardy garden plant in mild temperate climates with a thick winter mulch, though a frost-free cold frame remains the safest option in colder zones.

planting.note: Pot pseudobulbs in a gritty, free-draining mix in mid-to-late summer as new roots begin to form, since Pleione praecox flowers in autumn rather than spring like most Pleione species; grow in a shaded, cool, frost-free greenhouse or bright indoor spot in zone 9-10, as it is more cold-sensitive than the widely grown P. formosana.

directions: Pot the pseudobulbs shallowly in a gritty, fast-draining mix in mid to late summer as fresh roots start to appear, then keep in a cool, shaded spot with rising humidity through autumn. Pleione praecox is unusual among cultivated Pleiones in flowering in autumn, before the new leaf has developed, sending up fragrant, pale to deep pink flowers with a frilled, blotched lip directly from the base of the previous season's pseudobulb, native to lithophytic and epiphytic sites in the eastern Himalaya and southwestern China. Because it flowers and grows later in the year than P. formosana, it needs a milder, frost-free winter rest and is generally grown as a container plant brought under cover rather than planted directly in a temperate garden bed. Reduce water gradually once flowering finishes and the leaf begins to die back, keeping the pseudobulb nearly dry and frost-free until active growth resumes the following summer.

planting.note: Mount on a small piece of cork bark or tree fern fiber, or pot in a shallow container of fine, fast-draining epiphytic mix; grow as a warm, humid houseplant or greenhouse specimen in zone 10-12, since Bulbophyllum frostii is a diminutive Vietnamese species that needs constant moisture at the roots but cannot tolerate a soggy mix.

directions: Mount on a small slab of cork bark or tree fern fiber, or grow in a shallow pot of fine, fast-draining bark mix, in bright shade with high, constant humidity. Bulbophyllum frostii is one of the smallest and most sought-after miniature Bulbophyllums in cultivation, a Vietnamese species whose tiny creeping rhizome carries small, closely spaced pseudobulbs each topped by a single leaf. Each pseudobulb produces a solitary flower that is disproportionately large relative to the plant, a brilliant star-shaped bloom in vivid red to orange-red with a fringed, mobile lip that quivers in the slightest breeze. Keep the mount or mix consistently damp without letting water stand around the tiny roots, since good drainage and steady humidity together, rather than either alone, are what this dwarf species needs to thrive and slowly spread across its support.

common_name: King Jewel Orchid (Golden Thread Orchid, Roxburgh's Anoectochilus)

planting.note: Grow as a terrarium or high-humidity windowsill specimen in zone 11-12; Anoectochilus roxburghii needs consistently high humidity (70%+), even moisture in a light, peat- or sphagnum-based terrestrial mix, and cannot tolerate frost, dry indoor air, or direct sun.

directions: Grow in a humid terrarium, glass cloche, or enclosed vivarium in deep shade, potted in a light, evenly moist mix of sphagnum moss and fine bark or coir. Anoectochilus roxburghii is a terrestrial jewel orchid from the forest floors of southern China, Vietnam, and Japan, grown for its dark, velvety, blackish-green leaves netted with fine coppery-red to gold veining rather than for its small, inconspicuous white flowers. Long valued in traditional Chinese medicine under names translating to 'king medicine' or 'golden thread grass,' it is now also widely propagated as an ornamental foliage plant for terrariums alongside the closely related Ludisia and Macodes. Provide consistently high humidity and gentle, indirect light, since strong sun quickly scorches the delicate leaves, and keep the growing mix evenly moist but never waterlogged around its shallow, creeping stems.

planting.note: Grow bare-root or in a slatted teak basket with little or no medium, hung where the thick silver roots get maximum air movement; Vanda 'Pachara Delight' is a warmth-loving modern hybrid grown outdoors year-round only in zone 10-12 and needs to be brought inside or into a heated greenhouse elsewhere.

directions: Grow bare-root in a hanging slatted basket or clay pot with little to no medium so the thick silver-white aerial roots stay exposed to moving air, providing very bright, filtered light and daily wetting followed by rapid drying. Vanda 'Pachara Delight' is one of the most widely propagated modern Vanda hybrids, produced by the thousands at Thai orchid nurseries for its rounded, richly colored violet-blue to purple flowers marked with a darker net of veining, borne in long-lasting sprays that can appear nearly year-round in warm, bright conditions. Like its wild Vanda parents, it is a monopodial epiphyte with no pseudobulbs to store water, so the roots need frequent misting or dunking in warm weather and must dry within a few hours to avoid rot. This hybrid is a familiar sight in Southeast Asian markets, resorts, and the cut-flower trade, valued for its reliable, heavy flowering and relatively compact size compared with many strap-leaf Vanda species.

common_name: Terete Vanda (Cylindrical-Leaved Orchid, formerly Vanda teres)

planting.note: Plant at the base of a sturdy post, trellis, or living tree in full sun so the scrambling stems have something to climb, using a coarse, fast-draining mix or bare-root wiring; Papilionanthe teres (formerly Vanda teres) needs more direct sun than almost any other orchid and is grown outdoors year-round only in zone 10-12.

directions: Plant at the base of a sturdy stake, trellis, or living tree in full, unfiltered sun, tying or wiring the climbing stems as they grow so they can scramble upward the way they would over a host tree in the wild. Papilionanthe teres, long known as Vanda teres, is immediately recognizable by its round, pencil-like, jointed leaves that lack the flat blade typical of most orchids, an adaptation associated with the intensely sunny, well-drained slopes and riverbanks of India, Myanmar, and Thailand where it grows. Large, fragrant, rose-pink and white flowers with a golden-yellow, red-veined lip appear from the leaf axils of mature growths, typically in warm weather, on a plant that tolerates more direct sun than nearly any other commonly grown orchid. Because it has no pseudobulbs and needs strong light to flower well, it performs best planted directly in the ground or a large slatted basket outdoors in frost-free climates rather than as a windowsill houseplant.

common_name: Scarlet Renanthera (Red Fire Orchid, Christmas Orchid)

planting.note: Plant against a strong trellis, post, or tree trunk in full sun, since Renanthera coccinea is a large, vigorous, climbing monopodial orchid whose stem can eventually reach many feet in length; grow outdoors year-round only in zone 10-12, or as a large greenhouse specimen elsewhere.

directions: Provide full, direct sun and a sturdy trellis, post, or tree to climb, since Renanthera coccinea is a vigorous, sprawling, monopodial orchid native to Vietnam, Laos, and southern China whose wiry stem lengthens year after year and eventually needs substantial support. Established plants produce branched sprays of numerous brilliant, waxy, scarlet-red flowers with narrow, twisted petals, a fade-resistant color so intense that the species has long been used as a parent in breeding red-flowered orchid hybrids across several related genera. It demands more light than almost any Cattleya or Vanda to flower well, along with a coarse, fast-draining mount or basket and regular watering that dries quickly, since standing moisture around the roots invites rot. Because of its size and climbing habit, Renanthera coccinea is best suited to an outdoor trellis in frost-free gardens or a tall greenhouse rather than a small pot on a windowsill.

planting.note: Mount on rough bark or grow in a slatted basket with coarse, fast-draining mix in bright indirect to partial direct sun; Encyclia alata is native from Mexico to Costa Rica and Venezuela and needs a distinct, drier winter rest to flower and pseudobulb well, performing best outdoors year-round in zone 9-11.

directions: Mount on rough bark or grow in a slatted basket with a coarse, fast-draining bark mix in bright indirect to partial direct sun with good air movement around the roots. Encyclia alata ranges from Mexico south through Central America to Venezuela and forms notably large, egg-shaped pseudobulbs for the genus, each carrying a tall, branched flower spike of numerous fragrant, yellow-green blooms heavily overlaid with maroon-brown blotching around a contrasting white, three-lobed lip. It is considered one of the easiest and most floriferous Encyclia species to grow, tolerating a wider range of light and watering than many relatives while still rewarding growers with a long, showy display. Water regularly through active growth in spring and summer, then cut back sharply in fall and winter to give the pseudobulbs the pronounced dry rest they need to trigger the next season's flower spike.
